evic1-they-turn-the-needy-out-of-the-way.reason: Opens on what kind of text Job 24 is; the title's answer (the Word looks at dispossession at ground level, in the cold, so we see it that way before any rule) is only stated in the closing lines.
evic1-they-turn-the-needy-out-of-the-way.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does Job refuse to look away from a family put out in the cold? Because his account does not stop where our paperwork stops, at the handing over of keys. It walks out with the people and tells you where they slept and how cold it was (Job 24:7), and the Word preserved it. Before you learn any rule about evictions, you learn to look at it the way the Word looks. Here is what Job shows.
evic1-they-turn-the-needy-out-of-the-way.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does Job refuse to look away, and why does this come before the rules? Because the Word looks at dispossession exactly: the moved landmark, the widow's ox taken (Job 24:2-3), the needy turned out and hiding together (Job 24:4), the night without covering in the cold (Job 24:7). Job is a suffering man speaking, not a ruling from the whirlwind, yet his description stands. Rules that start without that sight start in the wrong place. So you stand at ground level first, with the people who are hiding together, and then you learn the rules.

teen.open: Why does Job keep looking at families thrown out into the cold? Because the Word does not stop at the paperwork. It follows the people out the door.
teen.close: So why look first, before the rules? Because rules mean little until you see the real people in the cold. The Word shows you where they slept.

senior.open: The title asks why Job will not look away from a family put out in the cold. His account does not end at the handover of keys; it follows the people into the night, and the Word preserved it.
senior.close: So the answer is this. Before any rule, the Word teaches a way of seeing: at ground level, with the dispossessed, in the cold. Job speaks as a suffering man, yet his description is exact, and it sets the posture every rule must start from.

evic2-cast-out-from-their-pleasant-house.reason: Answers at once from Micah 2:9 (YE cast out: Yahweh names the doer, not the market), but closes on a classroom exercise and the next lessons rather than on who did the evicting.
evic2-cast-out-from-their-pleasant-house.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who did the evicting? Micah 2:9 answers in the second person: ye cast out. Yahweh does not call it a market outcome or a regrettable necessity. It is an act with a doer, and He names the doer. The houses were pleasant homes, not units, and He speaks of what was taken from the children as His own glory. Then the words of eviction come back on the evictors (Micah 2:10). Whoever holds the notice cannot hide behind the process.

teen.open: Who is responsible when a family is thrown out of their home? In Micah 2:9, Yahweh points straight at the people who did it: you did.
teen.close: So who did the evicting? Not the system. The people doing it. Yahweh names them, and that should make anyone holding a notice stop and think.

senior.open: The title asks who did the evicting. Micah 2:9 answers plainly in the second person: ye have cast out. Yahweh names the doer rather than blaming circumstance.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. In Micah 2 the removal is an act with a doer, and Yahweh speaks of it as touching His own glory. The one holding the notice is named, and cannot shelter behind process or market.

evic5-the-year-to-redeem.reason: Shows the doubled 'full year' early, but why both ends are set in advance (an open window hands the decision to the stronger party; the clock must be the same for all) arrives in the last third; ends on a task.
evic5-the-year-to-redeem.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why did Yahweh set both ends of the window in advance? Because a window with no stated end does not stay open. The decision just moves to whoever has more power, who ends it on a day of his own choosing, without warning. Leviticus 25 states the start, states a full year twice, and states what happens when it runs out, to everyone, the same. Here is how the passage works.
evic5-the-year-to-redeem.example: TWO WAYS TO SAY IT. Say a landlord tells a struggling tenant to take whatever time he needs. It sounds kind. Then one bad week he has had enough and the tenant has days to leave, with no warning. Now say he writes instead: you have until a stated date; here is what happens if it is met, and what happens if it is not. The tenant can plan, call ahead, and act while time remains.
evic5-the-year-to-redeem.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why set both ends of the window in advance? So the weaker party can see the clock. Leviticus 25:29 gives a whole year, then a full year, so no one can argue later about what was meant, and verse 30 says plainly what happens when it closes. Where a house is someone's whole provision, as for the Levites, the right never expires (Leviticus 25:32). A righteous deadline is declared at both ends ahead of time, and kept at both ends, the same for the people you like and the people you do not.

teen.open: Why did Yahweh set a clear start and end for buying back a house? Because a deadline nobody states gets decided later by whoever has more power.
teen.close: So why both ends? A clear deadline, given ahead of time and kept the same for everyone, is fairer than a vague promise that can end any day.

senior.open: The title asks why Yahweh fixed both ends of the redemption window beforehand. An unstated end passes the decision to the stronger party; a declared one lets the weaker party plan.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Leviticus 25 states the year twice and states its end, and it keeps the Levites' right open because those houses were their whole provision. A righteous deadline is declared at both ends and honoured equally for all.

evic4-he-taketh-a-mans-life-to-pledge.reason: Explains the millstone first; the why (taking the means of daily bread is taking a man's life to pledge, anchored in remembering Egypt) builds through the middle; ends on a practical list rather than the answer gathered.
evic4-he-taketh-a-mans-life-to-pledge.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why does Yahweh put a family's daily bread off the table, even when a debt is owed? Because taking the thing a household eats by is not taking a possession. Deuteronomy 24:6 says it is taking a man's life to pledge. Some things may not be taken at any price, for any debt. And the reason Yahweh gives for keeping that law is memory: you were the slave He redeemed. Here is how the Word draws the line.
evic4-he-taketh-a-mans-life-to-pledge.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why is a family's daily bread off the table even when a debt is owed? Because the millstone, both stones, is the household's life, and taking it is taking a life as a pledge (Deuteronomy 24:6). The protection grows stronger where the person is weaker: a widow's raiment may not be taken at all (Deuteronomy 24:17). And the law rests on remembering that Yahweh redeemed you (Deuteronomy 24:18). So before taking anything, ask what it is for. The van, the tools, the phone the job calls: those are millstones, and they stay.

teen.open: Why won't Yahweh let a lender take the things a family needs to eat, even if they owe money? Because He says taking them is like taking a person's life.
teen.close: So why is daily bread off the table? Because a family's tools for living are their life. Yahweh rescued you when you had nothing, so you leave others' lifelines alone.

senior.open: The title asks why Yahweh removes a family's daily bread from what may be taken for debt. Deuteronomy 24:6 gives His reason: to take the millstone is to take a man's life to pledge.
senior.close: So the answer is plain. The means of a household's daily bread are outside every negotiation, and the protection grows strongest where the debtor is weakest. Yahweh grounds it in remembrance of His own redemption, which is what keeps a creditor's hand still.

evic6-took-him-by-the-throat.reason: Walks the parable in order; the title's question (can you hear your own plea in the other man's mouth) is only posed in the last lines, and the lesson ends on the servant who recognized nothing, not on the answer for you.
evic6-took-him-by-the-throat.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. When you hold the notice, can you still recognize your own plea in someone else's mouth? You must, and this parable shows why. The forgiven servant heard the very words he had begged with, "Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all", and they did not reach him. The King's charge was not about the money owed; it was about compassion he should have had. Here is how Matthew 18 shows it.
evic6-took-him-by-the-throat.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Can you still recognize your plea in someone else's mouth? That is exactly what the King required (Matthew 18:33). The servant asked for time and received cancellation, then heard his own words said back to him and would not listen (Matthew 18:29-30). This does not abolish lawful collection; the hundred pence was really owed. It asks something sharper: when the person across the table says what you once said on your knees, hear it as your own, and let what you were given shape what you do. Jesus says this forgiveness must come from the heart (Matthew 18:35).

teen.open: If someone begs you for more time, the same way you once begged, will you notice? In this story, a forgiven servant heard his own words and did not care.
teen.close: So can you hear your own plea in someone else? You need to. When you have been shown mercy, let it change how you treat the next person who asks.

senior.open: The title asks whether, holding the notice, you can still recognize your own plea in another's mouth. In Matthew 18 the forgiven servant heard his very words repeated to him and was unmoved.
senior.close: So the answer is this. The parable does not cancel lawful claims, but it charges the one who was shown pity to have compassion in turn. When your own words come back to you from across the table, hear them as yours.

evic7-jobs-own-oath.reason: Opens on the oath's form; what Job 31 actually asks a landlord (did you hear their grievances, use the law against the fatherless, gain by anyone's loss) is spread across the body and gathered only implicitly at the end.
evic7-jobs-own-oath.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does Job 31 ask a landlord before anyone else is judged? It asks you to put yourself under the standard first. Did you treat a grievance against you as worth hearing? When the law was on your side, did you use it against someone with no defender? Did anyone lose by the way you came to hold what you hold? Job swears to these against himself, because one Maker made you both. Here is how he does it.
evic7-jobs-own-oath.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Job 31 ask a landlord before anyone else is judged? It asks the landlord first. Not whether anyone complained, but how you handled it when they did (Job 31:13). Whether you held back your hand when you could see the judgment going your way (Job 31:21), because lawful and righteous are not the same thing. Whether anyone lost by how you came to hold the ground (Job 31:39). And the reason is one Maker who fashioned you both (Job 31:15). The standard goes inward before it goes outward.

teen.open: Before judging anyone else, what does Job ask himself? Did I listen when people complained? Did I use the rules to hurt someone weaker?
teen.close: So what does Job 31 ask? Check yourself first. The same Maker made you and the person you are dealing with.

senior.open: The title asks what Job 31 requires of a landlord before anyone else is judged. Job puts himself under oath first: how he heard complaints, whether he used his power at the gate, and whether anyone lost by his holding.
senior.close: So the answer stands. Job turns the standard inward first, grounded in one Maker of master and servant alike. Having the law on your side is not the same as being righteous, and the examination begins with you.

evic8-restored-to-the-debtor-his-pledge.reason: Ezekiel 18:7 shows what a righteous creditor gives back early, but Amos's charge comes late, and the lesson ends on a course recap, a task and a word to borrowers, not on the title's answer.
evic8-restored-to-the-debtor-his-pledge.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What does a righteous creditor give back, and what does Amos charge against those who keep it? He gives back the pledge, and Ezekiel lists that beside feeding the hungry as part of what righteousness is (Ezekiel 18:7). Amos charges men who lie down on garments taken in pledge, by every altar, in the very posture of worship (Amos 2:8). Here are the two portraits.
evic8-restored-to-the-debtor-his-pledge.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does a righteous creditor give back, and what is the charge against those who keep it? He gives back the pledge. Ezekiel puts it on the same list as feeding the hungry and covering the naked, and the standard holds a generation later (Ezekiel 18:7, 16). Amos shows the other side: the covering owed back to a cold man lying under a worshipper (Amos 2:8). Your conduct as a creditor is part of your righteousness, not a separate compartment. So give back what was laid in pledge, now.

teen.open: What does a good lender give back? The thing the borrower handed over as a promise. And Amos calls out people who keep it and even sit on it in worship.
teen.close: So what does a righteous lender give back? What belongs to the borrower. How you treat people who owe you is part of how you follow Yahweh.

senior.open: The title asks what a righteous creditor returns and what Amos charges against those who keep it. Ezekiel 18:7 counts restoring the pledge as righteousness; Amos 2:8 condemns men reclining on pledged garments by the altar.
senior.close: So the answer is settled. The righteous creditor restores the pledge, and Scripture places that beside feeding the hungry. Keeping it, even while worshipping, is the charge Amos brings. A lender's conduct belongs on the same list as his devotion.

evic3-thou-shalt-stand-abroad.reason: Opening states the answer (the debt and pledge stand; the law restrains only the method of collection and the hold) and the final paragraph lands it: nothing voids the loan, the lender stays outside and returns the pledge.
